type:0-0-0-0-t1.title: Count the Pictures
prerequisites: Say number names in order.
teachingSteps: Point to one object as you say one number.
Count each object once.
The last number tells how many objects there are.

workedExamples.question: Count these dots: ● ● ● ● ● ● ●
steps: Touch each dot once while saying 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7.

commonMistakes.mistake: Counting an object twice changes the total.
commonMistakes.guidance: Can you recount in a different direction and get the same total?

parentPrompts: Can you recount in a different direction and get the same total?
Which step explains your answer?
Can you apply the same reasoning when the numbers change?
type:0-0-0-0-t1.practiceAdvice: Work through the example together. Ask the learner to explain the first two problems, then try three independently. Review the first incorrect step before assigning more practice.
nextSteps: Use New Numbers to practice the same skill with different values.
If the learner needs help, return to the example and model each step before trying again.
type:0-0-0-0-t1.overview: Focus: Counting and Matching Numbers 1–9. Use the worked example and teaching sequence below to explain the reasoning before independent practice.

type:0-0-0-0-t2.title: Match Pictures and Numbers
prerequisites: Say number names in order.
teachingSteps: Count each pictured group to find its number.
Match each picture to the numeral with the same value.
Check the match by recounting the picture.

workedExamples.question: Match each picture to its number: ● ● ●  →  2, 3, 4
steps: Connect this picture to 3 because both represent three.

commonMistakes.mistake: Matching a picture to a numeral without counting the objects.
commonMistakes.guidance: Count the objects in this picture. Which numeral names that total?

parentPrompts: How many objects are in this group?
How can you check that the numeral and picture show the same amount?
What changes if one object is added?
type:0-0-0-0-t2.practiceAdvice: Work through the example together. Ask the learner to explain the first two problems, then try three independently. Review the first incorrect step before assigning more practice.
nextSteps: Use New Numbers to practice the same skill with different values.
If the learner needs help, return to the example and model each step before trying again.
type:0-0-0-0-t2.overview: Focus: Matching pictured quantities to numerals from 1 to 9. Model counting each group before drawing a match.

type:0-0-0-0-t3.title: Draw the Given Number
prerequisites: Say number names in order.
teachingSteps: Read the numeral first.
Color or mark exactly that many objects.
Count the marked objects to check the quantity.

workedExamples.question: Color 5 circles: ○ ○ ○ ○ ○ ○
steps: Count five circles from left to right and color them.

commonMistakes.mistake: Coloring one too many or one too few objects.
commonMistakes.guidance: Count only the colored circles. Do you have exactly five?

parentPrompts: What number are you showing?
How many circles should be colored?
How can you check the count?
type:0-0-0-0-t3.practiceAdvice: Work through the example together. Ask the learner to explain the first two problems, then try three independently. Review the first incorrect step before assigning more practice.
nextSteps: Use New Numbers to practice the same skill with different values.
If the learner needs help, return to the example and model each step before trying again.
type:0-0-0-0-t3.overview: Focus: Showing a given number by coloring or marking that many objects. Have the learner read the numeral, make the set, and recount it.

type:0-0-0-0-t4.title: Complete the Number Sequence
prerequisites: Say number names in order.
teachingSteps: Read the numbers in order.
Find the step between consecutive numbers.
Continue that pattern through the blank and check the sequence.

workedExamples.question: Complete the sequence: 2, 3, □, 5
steps: The numbers increase by 1 each time.

commonMistakes.mistake: Skipping a number or counting the starting number as the next step.
commonMistakes.guidance: Say the sequence aloud one number at a time. What comes immediately after 3?

parentPrompts: How does each number change?
Which number comes just before the blank?
Does your answer keep the sequence in order?
type:0-0-0-0-t4.practiceAdvice: Work through the example together. Ask the learner to explain the first two problems, then try three independently. Review the first incorrect step before assigning more practice.
nextSteps: Use New Numbers to practice the same skill with different values.
If the learner needs help, return to the example and model each step before trying again.
type:0-0-0-0-t4.overview: Focus: Completing a counting sequence from 1 to 9. Use the neighboring numbers to identify the missing number.

type:0-0-0-1-t1.title: Write 0 for an Empty Set
prerequisites: Count forward and backward.
teachingSteps: Count the objects shown in the picture.
If the set is empty, no objects are present, so its count is zero.
Check that the written numeral represents the pictured quantity.

workedExamples.question: Count the apples in an empty basket: [empty]
steps: There are no apples to count.
A set with no objects has a count of 0.

commonMistakes.mistake: Writing 1 because the empty picture itself is one object.
commonMistakes.guidance: Count the objects inside the picture. Are there any apples?

parentPrompts: How many objects are in the picture?
What numeral represents none?
What would change if one object were added?
type:0-0-0-1-t1.practiceAdvice: Work through the example together. Ask the learner to explain the first two problems, then try three independently. Review the first incorrect step before assigning more practice.
nextSteps: Use New Numbers to practice the same skill with different values.
If the learner needs help, return to the example and model each step before trying again.

type:0-0-0-1-t2.title: Match Picture Counts to 0–9
prerequisites: Count forward and backward.
teachingSteps: Count the objects in each picture, including an empty picture as zero.
Match each picture to the numeral with the same value.
Recount one matched picture to verify the connection.

workedExamples.question: Match the picture to its number: ● ● ●  →  2, 3, 4
steps: Connect it to 3, which names the same quantity.

commonMistakes.mistake: Matching by the appearance or position of a numeral instead of its value.
commonMistakes.guidance: Count the objects in the picture. Which numeral represents that count?

parentPrompts: How many objects are shown?
Which numeral has the same value?
How would an empty picture be matched?
type:0-0-0-1-t2.practiceAdvice: Work through the example together. Ask the learner to explain the first two problems, then try three independently. Review the first incorrect step before assigning more practice.

type:0-0-0-1-t3.title: Complete Sequences from 0 to 9
prerequisites: Count forward and backward.
teachingSteps: Read the sequence from left to right.
Determine how the numbers change from one position to the next.
Use that pattern to fill the blank and check both neighbors.

workedExamples.question: Complete the sequence: 0, 1, □, 3
steps: The sequence increases by 1 each time.
The number after 1 is 2, and 2 is followed by 3.

commonMistakes.mistake: Starting the count at 1 when the sequence begins at 0.
commonMistakes.guidance: Read every shown number from the beginning. What comes after 1?

parentPrompts: What is the pattern from one number to the next?
What number comes after 1?
Does the completed sequence include every number in order?
type:0-0-0-1-t3.practiceAdvice: Work through the example together. Ask the learner to explain the first two problems, then try three independently. Review the first incorrect step before assigning more practice.
nextSteps: Use New Numbers to practice the same skill with different values.
If the learner needs help, return to the example and model each step before trying again.
type:0-0-0-1-t3.overview: Focus: Completing number sequences from 0 to 9. Identify the counting pattern and use it to fill the missing position.

type:0-0-0-1-t4.title: Numbers Before and After
prerequisites: Count forward and backward.
teachingSteps: Read the given number.
Find the number immediately before it and the number immediately after it.
Check by counting forward and backward one step.

workedExamples.question: Write the number before and the number after 5: □, 5, □
steps: Count back one from 5 to get 4.
Count forward one from 5 to get 6.

commonMistakes.mistake: Writing 5 itself in one of the neighboring positions.
commonMistakes.guidance: Move one count backward for the first blank and one count forward for the second.

parentPrompts: What comes just before 5?
What comes just after 5?
How can you check each neighbor?
type:0-0-0-1-t4.practiceAdvice: Work through the example together. Ask the learner to explain the first two problems, then try three independently. Review the first incorrect step before assigning more practice.
nextSteps: Use New Numbers to practice the same skill with different values.
If the learner needs help, return to the example and model each step before trying again.

type:0-0-0-1-t5.title: Missing Numbers on a Number Line
prerequisites: Count forward and backward.
teachingSteps: Read the labeled numbers on the number line.
Determine the counting interval between tick marks.
Use that interval to identify and write the number at the blank tick.

workedExamples.question: Fill the missing number on the number line: 0 — 1 — □ — 3
steps: The tick after 1 and before 3 is 2.

commonMistakes.mistake: Counting tick marks instead of the spaces between them.
commonMistakes.guidance: Start at the labeled tick 0 and move one space at a time. What number is at the blank tick?

parentPrompts: What value does each tick mark represent?
How many spaces from 0 to the blank?
Does the answer fit between the neighboring labels?

teachingSteps: Count the objects in each picture, grouping ten objects when helpful.

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting to include the objects left after making a group of ten.
commonMistakes.guidance: After counting ten, how many dots remain? Add them to ten.

parentPrompts: How many full groups of ten are shown?

prerequisites: Say number names in order.
teachingSteps: Read the numeral and identify how many objects it represents.
Make a group of ten when the number is at least ten.
Color or mark the remaining objects and recount the full set.

workedExamples.question: Color 14 circles: ○ ○ ○ ○ ○ ○ ○ ○ ○ ○ ○ ○ ○ ○ ○
steps: Color ten circles as one group.

commonMistakes.mistake: Coloring only the ones digit in a two-digit number.
commonMistakes.guidance: For 14, how many circles make the group of ten, and how many more are needed?

parentPrompts: How many objects make one group of ten?

type:0-2-0-0-t1.title: Choose an Equation for the Picture
prerequisites: Read the numbers and identify the operation.
teachingSteps: Start in the ones place and subtract corresponding places.
If a top digit is too small, exchange one unit from the next place for ten units in the current place.
Mark both changes: the giving place decreases by one and the receiving place increases by ten.
Continue left, using the changed digits.

commonMistakes.mistake: Do not reverse the digits just because the lower digit is larger. Subtraction keeps its original order. When a zero is involved, follow the exchange across the places rather than changing every zero independently.
commonMistakes.guidance: Add the difference to the number subtracted. You should recover the starting number.

type:0-2-3-5-t1.title: Find the Missing Number
prerequisites: Read the numbers and identify the operation.
teachingSteps: Start in the ones place and subtract corresponding places.
If a top digit is too small, exchange one unit from the next place for ten units in the current place.
Mark both changes: the giving place decreases by one and the receiving place increases by ten.
Continue left, using the changed digits.
For a blank, identify the missing quantity. Substitute the completed value back into the original statement to check it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Do not reverse the digits just because the lower digit is larger. Subtraction keeps its original order. When a zero is involved, follow the exchange across the places rather than changing every zero independently.

teachingSteps: Decide how many complete groups of the divisor fit into the current amount.
Write a quotient digit, multiply it by the divisor, and subtract.
Bring down the next digit and repeat.
A zero quotient digit may be needed to hold a place.
At the end, the remainder must be smaller than the divisor.

workedExamples.question: Find the quotient: 84 ÷ 4.
steps: Use multiples of 4 to find a quotient of 21.

commonMistakes.mistake: Do not stop just because a current digit is smaller than the divisor. Check whether more digits remain to be brought down. A remainder equal to or larger than the divisor means another complete group fits.
commonMistakes.guidance: Multiply the quotient by the divisor and add the remainder. This must equal the dividend.

parentPrompts: Multiply the quotient by the divisor and add the remainder. This must equal the dividend.
Which step explains your answer?
Can you apply the same reasoning when the numbers change?

teachingSteps: Write whole numbers over one and convert mixed numbers to improper fractions.
Multiply the numerators and multiply the denominators.
You may cancel common factors between a numerator and a denominator before multiplying, or simplify the product afterward.
A common denominator is not required for multiplication.
For a matching problem, solve each item before drawing its connection. Check that the connected representations have equal values.

commonMistakes.mistake: Do not multiply a mixed number’s whole part and fractional part separately and join them. Convert the entire mixed number first. Cancellation removes common factors, not digits that merely look alike.
commonMistakes.guidance: Estimate the size of each factor. A positive factor below one reduces the other positive factor. Check by dividing by a nonzero original factor.

parentPrompts: Estimate the size of each factor. A positive factor below one reduces the other positive factor. Check by dividing by a nonzero original factor.
Which step explains your answer?
Can you apply the same reasoning when the numbers change?
type:1-3-1-1-t3.practiceAdvice: Work through the example together. Ask the learner to explain the first two problems, then try three independently. Review the first incorrect step before assigning more practice.
nextSteps: Use New Numbers to practice the same skill with different values.
If the learner needs help, return to the example and model each step before trying again.

Multiply and simplify.

workedExamples.question: Evaluate (1 1/2)/(3).
steps: Rewrite each mixed number as an improper fraction: 1 1/2 = 3/2.

commonMistakes.guidance: Multiply the quotient by the original divisor, not its reciprocal. The result should equal the dividend.

variant:322.title: division worksheets beginner
prerequisites: Read the numbers and identify the operation.
teachingSteps: Decide how many complete groups of the divisor fit into the current amount.
Write a quotient digit, multiply it by the divisor, and subtract.
Bring down the next digit and repeat.
A zero quotient digit may be needed to hold a place.
At the end, the remainder must be smaller than the divisor.

workedExamples.question: Find the quotient: 24 ÷ 6.
steps: Use multiples of 6 to find a quotient of 4.

commonMistakes.mistake: Do not stop just because a current digit is smaller than the divisor. Check whether more digits remain to be brought down. A remainder equal to or larger than the divisor means another complete group fits.
commonMistakes.guidance: Multiply the quotient by the divisor and add the remainder. This must equal the dividend.
